```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.25)
```

Start with `vignette("bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` for annual
data preparation, full NUTS sampling and scientific interpretation. This guide
explains the alternative computations, what their diagnostics establish and
how to assess numerical precision. They use the same posterior target when
the likelihood, priors, formulas and prepared bins are held fixed.

## Use the worked example

The data are the five-year NB2 example from the annual-scale guide. Loading
the stored numeric inputs and compact NUTS fit requires no optional Bayesian
software. The long approximation calls below are shown rather than executed
while building the package.

```{r example-data}
example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
dat <- example$data
inputs <- example$inputs
response <- count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site)
scales <- list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year))
fit <- example$fits$pooled
```

For uncorrected approximations, check RTMB with
`check_bayes_setup("laplace")`. Importance correction also needs posterior:

```{r approximation-setup}
check_bayes_setup("marginal", correction = "importance")
```

`ready` describes package availability, not optimizer convergence, posterior
accuracy or available memory. Full NUTS is more general than the current
single-scale-SD marginal interface, but also needs its own raw and derived
diagnostics. Priors and data support must be assessed under every computation.

## Explore a joint Laplace approximation

Set `method = "laplace"` to replace MCMC with a Gaussian approximation around
a posterior mode. This option uses the same likelihood, priors, scale formulas,
and fixed predictor standardization as sampling. It requires RTMB, but does not
require tmbstan, rstan, or posterior.

```{r laplace-fit, eval=FALSE}
fast_fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  response, inputs, dat, scales = scales, row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2", priors = fit$specification$priors,
  method = "laplace", laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527001
)
summary(fast_fit)$diagnostics
posterior_scales(fast_fit)
summary(fast_fit)$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd
```

The approximation covers response coefficients, latent year and site effects,
log group SDs, and dispersion jointly. Its covariance is the inverse Hessian,
the matrix of second derivatives of the negative log posterior at the mode.
Complete correlated draws are transformed through the original scale formulas.
Pooling SDs retain uncertainty. This is a joint local approximation, rather
than a nested method that integrates out random effects.

The default uses six dispersed deterministic starts. `control = list(starts =
10, iter.max = 1500)` spends more effort searching for a stationary mode.
`laplace_draws` controls summary simulation error; increasing it cannot correct
an inaccurate Gaussian approximation. A supplied seed preserves your previous
random-number state. The sampling settings `chains`, `iter`, and `warmup` are
unused for this method.

**How to read the diagnostics:** `gradient_max` measures stationarity and must
not exceed 0.0001. `min_eigenvalue` must be positive and `condition_number` no
greater than one trillion for the covariance to be accepted. The function
reports an error instead of adjusting invalid curvature. `successful_starts`
counts converged stationary solutions. `competing_modes` flags distinct
solutions within two log-posterior units of the selected mode and causes a
warning. The starts are retained in `fast_fit$laplace$starts` for inspection.

These are numerical checks. A passed flag does not establish interval
calibration or accurate partial pooling. The approximation operates in
unconstrained, noncentered coordinates, including the log-SD Jacobians in the
prior. Its accuracy depends on that parameterization. Dependence between year
effects and their SD, skewness, and weak scale information can make a local
Gaussian misleading. Compare consequential annual-scale and pooling results
with full sampling, especially with few years or weak habitat effects. No
finite set of optimization starts guarantees that all posterior modes were
found.

## Integrate uncertainty in the between-year SD

The joint Gaussian approximation can misrepresent pooling even when its
optimizer converges. Use `method = "marginal"` to integrate one scale-group
SD numerically while fitting a conditional Laplace approximation for the other
parameters at each SD value. This allows an asymmetric SD posterior with mass
near zero. The likelihood and priors remain the same as for full sampling.

```{r marginal-fit, eval=FALSE}
marginal_fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  response, inputs, dat, scales = scales, row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2", priors = fit$specification$priors,
  method = "marginal", laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527002
)
summary(marginal_fit)$diagnostics
summary(marginal_fit)$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd
posterior_scales(marginal_fit)
```

At a fixed SD, the inverse conditional Hessian describes uncertainty in the
response effects, scale effects, and latent effects. Its determinant supplies
the conditional posterior volume needed when comparing different SD values.
Integration uses the half-normal prior's cumulative probability as its axis;
the change of coordinates removes the corresponding log-SD prior density
from the integrand so that the prior is counted exactly once. The method
then combines the conditional distributions with their integration weights.
SD draws are continuous, with conditional dependence retained through a
mixture of the neighboring integration configurations.

**How to read the diagnostics:** `grid_converged` checks whether refining
the integration grid changes the SD distribution appreciably. `refinement`
records changes in the CDF, central 95% interval and median, and log normalizing
constant. `competing_mass` is the approximate node probability associated with
discovered competing conditional modes; values above 0.01 fail the numerical
screen. `upper_tail_mass` checks that numerical integration has not accumulated
more than 0.001 posterior mass beyond prior cumulative probability 0.9999.
A failed conditional optimization causes an error instead of dropping its
integration point. Inspect all flags before interpreting the approximate draws.

The default refines grids up to 129 ordinary points, with additional points
in the upper prior tail. Set `control = list(max_grid = 257)` for a more
demanding integration check. Increasing `laplace_draws` only reduces simulation
error in the summaries. It cannot fix an inaccurate conditional Gaussian.

This implementation integrates exactly one scale-group SD, such as the
between-year SD in `~1 + (1 | year)`. Any response-site SD remains in the
conditional Gaussian approximation. Multiple scale-group SDs are not yet
supported by this method. It implements single-SD conditional Laplace integration. Numerical grid convergence does not
establish calibration, particularly with weak effects or multiple posterior
modes. Compare important results with NUTS.

## Correct conditional skewness with importance sampling

The SD grid can be accurate while conditional Gaussian annual intervals remain
too narrow. An experimental correction uses the marginal approximation to
propose parameter vectors, then weights each vector by the full posterior
density divided by its actual proposal density. It targets the same posterior
as NUTS. It does not multiply intervals by a fitted coverage adjustment.

```{r marginal-importance, eval=FALSE}
corrected_fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  response, inputs, dat, scales = scales, row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2", priors = fit$specification$priors,
  method = "marginal", laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527003,
  control = list(correction = "importance", conditional_beta = FALSE,
    nested_response = TRUE, importance_df = 5,
    importance_min = 65536, importance_max = 131072,
    importance_refinements = 2)
)
corrected_fit$diagnostics
corrected_fit$importance$history
corrected_fit$importance$proposal_diagnostics
posterior_scales(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted")
```

With response
random intercepts, correction defaults to nested response-effect integration.
This accounts for their conditional posterior volume when locating the other
parameters. With one response grouping term, the site-effect proposal is also
updated at every candidate's response SD. This avoids extending one Gaussian
description across all possible strengths of site variation.

A separate 16384-candidate pilot learns conditional proposal means and
covariances. It is discarded from final estimation. Production sampling mixes
the adapted proposal with the original heavy-tailed proposal, then evaluates
the unchanged joint posterior. The code retains 2000 resampled vectors by
default so that existing summary, prediction, and simulation methods work.
Those resamples share a finite weighted population. Their count is not an
effective sample size, and increasing `laplace_draws` cannot repair poor weights.

The proposal mixes Student t coordinates that can explore individually with a
multivariate Student t component that can explore jointly. A small uniform
component preserves support over the SD's prior-CDF axis, and a log-SD tail
proposal extends beyond the finite-precision inverse-CDF endpoint. Both
components are included in the importance density and do not change the prior.
The conditional proposal uses seven degrees of freedom by default.
`importance_df = 5` gives it heavier tails, which can cover posterior regions
that produce unstable ratios with the default proposal. The same exact
importance correction and diagnostic thresholds apply. This is an efficiency
choice: heavier tails can improve reliability but can also spend more
candidates in regions with little posterior mass. Check all diagnostics and
compare independent seeds before relying on the resulting intervals.
For difficult joint scale and response-coefficient geometry, an experimental
alternative is `conditional_beta = TRUE`. It draws response coefficients
conditional on each proposed set of scales and response random effects. For
Gaussian responses this conditional is exact. The other families use a local
Student t proposal; full importance ratios still target the same posterior.
A defensive component samples latent-scale parameters from the existing model
priors. This improves support without changing those priors.

```{r conditional-coefficient-control, eval=FALSE}
conditional_control <- list(
  correction = "importance", conditional_beta = TRUE, importance_df = 5,
  importance_min = 65536, importance_max = 131072,
  importance_refinements = 2
)
```

This mode uses the full joint grid and automatically selects
`nested_response = FALSE` unless specified. An explicit `TRUE` conflicts with
conditional coefficients. It can cost substantially more per candidate; use
NUTS when consequential tail probabilities remain unstable across runs.
Passing a minimum indicator ESS of 400 is a numerical screen, not a guarantee
of precise 2.5% or 97.5% endpoints. At probability 0.025, an indicator ESS of
400 corresponds to a CDF Monte Carlo SE of about 0.0078 under its variance
approximation. Missed regions can make even that estimate optimistic.
By default, one
failed production stage can train a further proposal; it is then discarded and
a fresh stage is sampled. `importance_refinements = 0` disables that extra
training, while 2 permits another stage. `importance_max` caps the final stage,
so total candidate evaluations can exceed that setting. Check
`production_candidates` when assessing cost.

**How to read these diagnostics:** `pareto_k` measures how extreme importance
ratios become; values above 0.7 fail the screen. `ess` must be at least 1000,
and `min_tail_ess` at least 400. A single candidate may hold at most 0.01 of the
total weight. `split_cdf_error` compares probability estimates from two
production halves and must be at most 0.05. `history` shows whether additional
candidates improved these checks. The original grid and mode flags remain in
`proposal_diagnostics`; they describe the proposal, while the new checks
describe the corrected estimate. Neither set proves that an unseen mode has
been found. Compare important or failed results with full NUTS.

Correction costs more than uncorrected marginal Laplace. It can be worthwhile
when conditional skewness matters and a stable proposal gives enough effective
samples quickly. Repeated-site models and weakly identified scales can still
be difficult. More than one response grouping term uses a joint proposal whose
reliability needs separate validation. The default `correction = "none"`
preserves the original marginal behavior.

## Compare actual computations of the worked example

These are the first attempts from the three calls above, with the complete
priors from the original NUTS fit. The package stores only their summary
tables and diagnostics, so this comparison needs no sampler or RTMB.

```{r actual-computation-status}
comparison <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-computation-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
knitr::kable(comparison$availability, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

`eligible` means the method passed its own stored numerical screen.
In these tables, `nested` labels the corrected marginal fit with the nested
response proposal; its function argument remains `method = "marginal"`.
Uncorrected marginal Laplace is retained as `rejected` because its SD grid
did not converge under the stated budget. Its intervals below illustrate
that failure; they are not accepted estimates. The timings describe these
particular computations on a shared computer, with different numerical
precision. They are not a benchmark of equal-precision methods.
The original NUTS fit recorded
`r round(example$fit_info$seconds[example$fit_info$model == "Hierarchical"], 1)`
seconds, so this example shows no elapsed-time advantage for correction.

```{r actual-annual-comparison, fig.height=5.5}
annual <- subset(comparison$quantiles, type == "annual_log_scale")
annual$method <- factor(annual$method,
  levels = c("nuts", "laplace", "marginal", "nested"),
  labels = c("NUTS reference", "Joint Laplace", "Marginal (rejected)",
    "Corrected marginal"))
ggplot2::ggplot(annual, ggplot2::aes(x = label, y = median,
    ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = method, shape = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .6)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Year", y = "Annual log distance: median and 95% interval",
    color = "Computation", shape = "Computation") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  ggplot2::guides(color = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))
```

The annual axis uses natural log distance. Exponentiating an estimate returns
map units. Joint Laplace places the annual medians higher than NUTS despite
passing its optimizer and curvature checks. Corrected marginal medians are
closer to the NUTS reference, although lower endpoints still differ. Both
computations have finite numerical precision, and this one example cannot
establish interval calibration.

```{r actual-sd-comparison}
sd_table <- subset(comparison$quantiles, type == "scale_sd",
  select = c(method, status, lower, median, upper))
knitr::kable(sd_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Between-year SD on the log-distance axis: marginal 95% intervals.")
```

The NUTS median SD is about 0.235; joint Laplace gives about 0.619 and the
corrected calculation about 0.230. The rejected marginal calculation gives
about 0.085. Integrating one SD does not automatically improve its estimate
when the remaining conditional approximation or integration is inadequate.
A positive lower interval limit does not test the exact hypothesis of no
annual variation: the continuous half-normal prior has no point mass at zero.

```{r actual-corrected-diagnostics}
unlist(comparison$diagnostics$nested[c("pareto_k", "ess", "min_tail_ess",
  "max_weight", "split_cdf_error")])
```

Read these against the fixed cutoffs above. The compact NUTS reference retains
2000 draw vectors from an original 12000 post-warmup draws; its original raw
and derived checks were assessed before compaction. These compact vectors
cannot reproduce chain-order diagnostics. The approximation SD table uses
direct importance weights for the corrected method and simulated quantiles
for the two uncorrected methods.

### Evidence beyond one example

On all 40 archived repeated-site simulation inputs, the nested response
proposal passed the unchanged importance checks for 19 of 20 Gaussian and
20 of 20 NB2 datasets. The conditional-coefficient alternative passed for
10 of 20 and 13 of 20, respectively. Original NUTS passed for 20 of 20 and
18 of 20. The remaining nested rejection had minimum indicator ESS 389,
below the required 400, and remains a rejection.

For the 19 Gaussian and 18 NB2 datasets where both nested correction and
NUTS passed, annual log-scale RMSE ratios were 0.999 and 1.002, and mean
95% interval-width ratios were 0.995 and 0.998. These reused-input comparisons
support this proposal choice for these tested models. They do not establish
equivalence, independent calibration, or reliability for crossed response
effects. Different eligibility sets must not be compared as if they contained
the same datasets.

## Separate posterior uncertainty from Monte Carlo uncertainty

A credible interval describes posterior uncertainty about a scale. Monte Carlo
uncertainty describes how accurately a finite computation estimates that
posterior interval or median. Passing convergence or importance diagnostics
does not guarantee a precise annual median. A flat posterior CDF near its
median can turn a small probability error into a substantial distance change.

For corrected fits, summarize the retained joint candidate population directly
to avoid the additional variability of multinomial resampling:

```{r weighted-scale-summary, eval=FALSE}
posterior_scales(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted")
posterior_scales(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted", scale = "log")
```

These summaries use the same posterior target and importance weights. They do
not improve candidate effective sample size or recover an unseen posterior
region. The weighted SD describes the finite weighted population. The earlier
cautions about infinite arithmetic distance moments still apply. Weighted
summaries require `draws = NULL`; the default estimator still uses stored
draws for every inference method. The plot method's automatic
estimator uses direct weights for corrected fits. To compare a table and
plot consistently, request `estimator = "weighted"` in both.

`importance_max` is a cap. A smaller population can pass diagnostics and stop
before reaching it. To require more production candidates, set a minimum too:

```{r importance-precision, eval=FALSE}
precision_control <- list(
  correction = "importance",
  importance_min = 65536, importance_max = 131072,
  importance_refinements = 2
)
# Pass precision_control to multiScale_bayes(..., method = "marginal", control = ...).
```

The default minimum is 16384; it must not exceed the maximum. Larger populations
cost more and do not guarantee a chosen quantile error. Inspect the retained
candidate count, diagnostics, and independently seeded results. When NUTS and
correction disagree, check both computations: extend sampling, compare seeds,
and assess mixing and quantile precision for the derived annual log scales.
The current NUTS eligibility flag checks unconstrained parameters and sampler
behavior; it does not certify annual-median Monte Carlo precision.

You can also check a probability that answers a specific question, such as
whether a fitted kernel scale is no greater than 250 map units:

```{r probability-precision}
probability_check <- diagnose_bayes_probabilities(fit,
  thresholds = list(habitat = c(100, 250)), mcse_target = 0.005)
probability_check$available
probability_check$reason
```

This compact teaching fit has no original sampler, so it cannot provide new
chain diagnostics. With the original NUTS sampler retained, `probabilities`
reports each fitted group's event probability, indicator ESS, Rhat and MCSE;
`chain_probabilities` shows differences among chains. The target of 0.005 is
half a percentage point of Monte Carlo standard error, not a credible interval width.
An indicator that stays at zero or one has nonestimable precision. It cannot
certify that an unseen tail is absent. Read this report alongside the original
diagnostics and `diagnose_bayes_scales()`; meeting an MCSE target does not replace
their checks. Thresholds refer to the kernel scale parameter, rather than an
automatically transformed radius containing a chosen share of kernel weight.

Indicator Rhat can be undefined for a balanced binary event even when its mean
ESS and MCSE are finite. The report keeps that Rhat as `NA`; `rhat_available`
and `rhat_reason` describe its availability. `precision_available` concerns
mean precision. A computable probability MCSE still requires the original
sampling and derived-scale checks before interpretation.

## Decision checklist

1. Keep likelihoods, priors, data alignment and predictor standardization fixed
   when comparing computations of the same posterior.
2. Inspect every method's own checks. Do not treat importance ESS as MCMC ESS,
   resampled draw counts as independent information, or a converged grid as
   evidence of calibrated annual intervals.
3. For NUTS, inspect `diagnose_bayes_scales()` using the original sampler.
   Compact or permuted draws cannot reconstruct chain-order diagnostics.
4. Compare annual quantiles and the pooling SD, including their numerical
   precision. Independent seeds can reveal instability, but do not discard a
   failed first attempt or claim that a favorable repeat establishes accuracy.
5. Assess response-model adequacy and prior sensitivity separately. None of
   these numerical checks establishes that a landscape scale is identified.

## Quick reference

```{r computation-reference, eval=FALSE}
check_bayes_setup("marginal", correction = "importance")
corrected_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat,
  scales = scales, row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
  priors = list(scale_median = 250), method = "marginal", seed = 521,
  control = list(correction = "importance"))
corrected_fit$diagnostics             # weight and probability-stability checks
corrected_fit$importance$history      # includes discarded training effort
posterior_scales(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted")
plot(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted")
# A failed flag calls for investigation or another computation, not weaker cutoffs.
```

| Output | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `fit$diagnostics` | Stored checks for the selected computation |
| `diagnose_bayes_scales(fit)` | Derived NUTS mixing and quantile MCSE when full chains exist |
| `diagnose_bayes_probabilities(fit, thresholds)` | Chain precision for specified fitted-scale probabilities |
| `fit$importance$proposal_diagnostics` | Original marginal grid and mode checks, separate from corrected weights |
| `fit$importance$history` | Production, adaptation and discarded-stage effort |
| `posterior_scales()` | Annual or shared distance quantiles, with explicit draw/weight estimator |

See also `vignette("bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` for the main
workflow, `vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for new
observations and years, and `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")`
for preparation. Prediction uses the stored joint vectors under every method,
including stored resamples for an importance-corrected fit. It does not add
posterior effective information or remove approximation error.
